items.action: Strabo described the Tagus as navigable by barges and river craft, with deep lower reaches that allowed the largest merchant transport ships to sail.
items.conditions: deep lower stretch of the river

items.action: Local Lusitanians used dugout canoes to cross and travel the estuary, an evolution from the leather boats seen during Brutus's expedition.
Father Fernando Oliveira noted that boat type names change over time and place, causing confusion; the same type has different names in different countries.
Oliveira observed that Santarém boats were raising their bows higher and changing their name from cervilhas to muletas, and that names like zabra and lancha were recent.
items.boat: barcos de Santarém (cervilhas, muletas), zabra, lancha

numbers.what: years since zabra and lancha names were unknown locally

items.action: Panoramic views of Lisbon by several artists, including an anonymous drawing at Leiden University, show Tagus boats, but later-period boats may be depicted in paintings of earlier events.
items.conditions: artistic views often lack scale or identification; anachronism risk
items.who: Francisco de Holanda, Amaro do Vale, Francisco Valégio

items.action: Manuel Fernandes's carpentry book gives layout methods and construction details for a falua and a fragata, likely built at the Ribeira and probably Tagus craft.
items.conditions: unclear whether they were Tagus boats
items.location: 1.2 – Bases de Dados de Imagens e seus Autores

items.action: João de Souza published a set of engravings of all Tagus boats, for cargo, transport and fishing, the first credible graphic record of Tagus boat types.
items.location: 1.2 – Bases de Dados de Imagens e seus Autores

items.action: J. S. Amancio published a technical plan of a closed-stern 'Hiate de Poupa fechada ou Carreira', intending to document all Tagus cargo and fishing boats; no continuation known.
items.boat: Hiate de Poupa fechada ou Carreira

items.action: Archivo Pittoresco began a series 'Marinha do Tejo' with Brito Aranha's descriptions of fishing and river transport boats, illustrated by J. Pedrozo's engravings, showing typological changes since 1785.
Spanish painter Raphael Monleón y Torres documented Portuguese boats, especially the muleta and the 'barino' (culé, colé, monaio, barco de água-acima).
items.boat: muleta; barino (culé, colé, monaio, barco de água-acima)

items.action: Admiral Pâris published Monleón's drawings of the muleta and barino in 'Souvenirs de Marine Conservés', described as the most extensive boat catalogue worldwide.

Unknown author Rascasço produced three notebooks of drawings, 'Costumes das nossas Embarcações', the most complete Tagus boat collection, showing side views with sails, above-waterline hulls, plan half-views and sections.
items.conditions: no scale; waterline missing in sections

items.action: Commander Baldaque da Silva published 'Estado Actual das Pescas', adding data on Tagus fishing boats, with perspective drawings, some descriptions and measurements.
items.who: Comandante António Artur Baldaque da Silva

items.action: A. J. Pinto Basto published 'As embarcações que navegam no Tejo' in Revista do Exército e da Armada, saying no prior study of Portuguese boats existed.
Pinto Basto notes sailors confused boat names, calling fragatas and varinos 'faluas'; the falua has two masts, the others one, and they serve very different purposes.
Henrique Maufroy de Seixas gathered a team of draughtsmen and model makers who recorded many boat types still in use and built precise models, now central to the Museu de Marinha.
Surviving traditional boats take part in annual regattas on the Tagus estuary, the last living examples of a once colourful riverside scene.
items.conditions: many boats lost to scrapping and abandonment

items.action: From the first quarter of the 20th century, researchers in ethnology and ethnography, later history and archaeology, began studying traditional boats.
Boats of the Middle Tagus worked river fishing, transport and crossings between Vila Velha de Rodão and Constância, using oars.
items.boat: flat-bottomed boats without stem post, transom stern
items.place: Vila Velha de Rodão to Constância

items.action: Cargo boats carried goods downstream from the Rossio, south of the Tagus, to the estuary and Lisbon, under lateen and staysail with a xarolo rudder.
items.boat: type D, curved stem and stern posts ending in bicas
items.gear: lateen sail, staysail, leme de xarolo
items.place: Rossio ao Sul do Tejo to Estuário-Lisboa

items.action: Lower Tagus boats did river fishing, transport and crossings between Constância and Santarém.
Avieira boats were used for river fishing and as dwellings between Santarém and Sacavém.
items.gear: oars, vela de pendão, vela de espicha, xarolo rudder

items.action: Lower Tagus boats are listed with types such as canoa, bateira, catrafuço, culé, barco do tráfego and varino, with dimensions given.
items.boat: canoa, bateira dos cagaréus, caçadeira avieira, barco do trá

items.action: Around Vila Franca de Xira, small boats did river fishing, carried fish and small goods, and ferried people.
items.place: Vila Franca de Xira area, Mouchões

items.action: Cargo boats carried goods upstream and downstream from Vila Franca de Xira; upstream boats lowered the mast to pass under the Marechal Carmona bridge.
items.place: Vila Franca de Xira, Ponte Marechal Carmona

items.action: Boats carried passengers between Cacilhas, Almada and Lisbon.
items.gear: oars, espicha, catita and jib sails

items.action: Larger keel boats carried people and cargo from Cacilhas to Ribatejo ports and the estuary's south bank.
items.boat: types C and D, keel boats
items.gear: carangueja and staysail, or two bastard sails
items.place: Cacilhas, Ribatejo ports, south bank of estuary

items.action: Tagus boats had smooth-plank hulls, keel or flat-bottomed, built by Mediterranean methods used since the 15th century or earlier.

numbers.what: identified types over about five centuries

items.action: Selected boat types are those surviving to the late active life of traditional boats, matching drawings and models of the Colecção Seixas in the Museu de Marinha.
The bote of the tapa-esteiros fishing art fished with support from the canoa das redes.
items.boat: bote da arte de tapa-esteiros, canoa das redes

items.action: Muleta and batel boats trawled from the side using the tartaranha net.
The batel replaced the muleta when the muleta became extinct.
Fast boats carried fish from muletas and batéis to destination ports while those vessels stayed anchored offshore or sheltered in estuary-mouth ports.
Describes a boat type with a keel, smooth planking, curved stem rising to the waterline then straight, a straight raked sternpost and a transom stern.
Lists propulsion and steering: lateen sail, bastard sail and jib, catita sail, eight auxiliary sails for managing trawling, esparrela oar and xarolo rudder.
items.gear: vela latina, vela de bastardo, bujarrona, catita, remo de esparrela, leme de xar

items.action: The Tagus is divided into five sectors, with the estuary split into three sub-sectors, from Alto Tejo down to the river mouth between Cabo Raso and Cabo Espichel.
items.place: Alto Tejo, Médio Tejo, Baixo Tejo, Estuário, Embocadura

items.action: Upper Tagus has no riverside settlements, so boats are very rare or absent; any present are picareto type.
Middle Tagus boats look primitive, but from Rossio ao Sul do Tejo long-distance boats carried local and regional products to the estuary, notably Lisbon.
items.place: Médio Tejo, Rossio ao Sul do Tejo, Lisboa

items.action: Avieiros, from Praia da Vieira, fished almost exclusively in the river, living aboard bateiras or in stilt-house villages they created.
In the Mouchões, some Avieiros remain, but the main activity is traffic and freight transport, partly in boats native to Vila Franca de Xira.
Varinos are small, shallow-draught boats traditionally using lateen and stay sails, able to navigate shallow ditches and creeks; lateen was later replaced by gaff sail.
items.gear: vela latina, vela de estai, vela de carangueja

items.action: Mar da Palha is the widest, hardest-to-navigate part of the estuary, so boats are sturdier and faster, mainly fragateiro rig with gaff sail and one or two stay sails.
items.gear: vela de carangueja, velas de estai

items.action: The main traditional shipyards are on the south bank of the Mar da Palha, where skilled local populations of varied origins work in nautical activities.
Foz and Embocadura are devoted to sea fishing, with fishermen from all over Portugal, including Galicians.
Fishing boats there are either keeled with transom stern, suggesting southern origin, or double-ended flat-bottomed, typical of the Aveiro lagoon.
Muletas are registered at south-bank ports such as Barreiro and Seixal but fish in the Embocadura waters called Entre-Cabos.
Valencian-style fixed fishing set-ups, some deep-sea fishing boats, coasters like caíques and rascas, and canoas da picada are not counted as Tagus boats, being built elsewhere.
Most listed boats have disappeared because of changes in transport and fishing and the notorious law ordering vessels to be scrapped; some survive, mostly sailing.
